# The Slow Leak of the Day

Every day, the Earth is losing a little time to the Moon.

The mechanism is tidal friction. The Moon's gravity raises bulges in the oceans, and as the planet spins beneath them, those bulges are dragged slightly ahead of the Moon's position. The bulges pull back on the Moon, speeding it up a little, and the Moon responds by moving into a higher orbit. Meanwhile, the Earth's rotation slows by a tiny amount, because it gave up some of its angular momentum to lift the Moon. The Moon drifts away at about 3.8 centimeters a year, roughly the speed your fingernails grow.

Nobody notices this in a lifetime. But the record is written in stone. Some fossil corals grow daily layers, like tree rings, with thicker bands for the summer and thinner ones for winter. Paleontologists who count those daily growth lines in Devonian corals, around 400 million years old, find about 400 days in a year. The year didn't have more days. Each day was shorter, closer to 21 or 22 hours, so the planet turned faster and there was more of them. The Moon was closer, and its tides were stronger.

I find this quietly staggering. We usually think of time as the fixed backdrop against which things happen, the thing that is simply there. But the length of a day is a negotiation between two bodies that are still, slowly, renegotiating. The ocean's rising and falling is a kind of friction, and the friction is a kind of accounting, and somewhere in the ledger a few hours have been moved from the Earth's column to the Moon's.

There's something comforting in the fact that the change is so gradual it never feels like change at all. A coral polyp in the Devonian sea laid down its little ridges, one per day, not knowing it was keeping a record of a world with a different clock. Eventually the stone it built became a document, and then a puzzle, and now a reason to say that the day you're having is not the day the dinosaurs had, or even the day your grandparents had, not quite.

In a few billion years the Moon will have drifted far enough, and the Earth's spin slowed enough, that the two will be locked into a single slow dance, and a day will last as long as a month. Eclipses will stop. The tides will ease. Whatever is alive then will have a calendar we can't imagine.

I like that the clock is not fixed. I like that the most reliable thing we know, the turning of the planet, is also a thing that is being spent, one centimeter at a time, on the Moon.
